newsitem.title: INDIA: India's PM backs troubled Agni missile project.
newsitem.headline: India's PM backs troubled Agni missile project.

text.p: Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Tuesday promised technical support to India's controversial Agni missile programme, weeks after the project appeared to have been shelved because of Western opposition.
The intermediate-range missile, believed capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, has a range of 2,500 km (1,500 miles) and is seen as a potential deterrent to China.

On Tuesday, Deve Gowda told the lower house of parliament his centre-left United Front coalition backed continuing research on the surface-to-surface missile, Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted him as saying.
"So far as necessary support to scientists is concerned -- full support," Deve Gowda said, after hardline nationalist opposition deputies questioned the government's commitment to the project.
In December, the decision to shelve the project was quietly conveyed in a Defence Ministry report to parliament.
The ministry said research on the rocket had been completed after three tests ending in early 1994, and there were no plans to produce the 14-tonne, 19-metre (60-foot) Agni.

The decision to put the missile on hold drew stinging criticism from the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and appeared bound to revive a simmering debate over the nation's ambiguous nuclear arms policy.
But the ministry said the government reserved the option to build the missile if India's security was threatened.
Analysts said the decision was linked to U.S.-led opposition to India's missile programme, which Washington says could upset regional stability.
The Agni is considered a potential deterrent against China, which is a declared nuclear weapons power.
India's 250-km (150-mile) Prithvi missile is regarded as more suited as a deterrent against neighbouring Pakistan, which is suspected of having the ability to quickly assemble nuclear weapons.
The decision to shelve the Agni was made public only days after Chinese President Jiang Zemin visited India.
Analysts said the defence ministry's report to parliament was written in August, well before Jiang's trip, but the timing of the news still raised eyebrows.
The BJP accused Deve Gowda's centre-left government, which has sought to improve ties with India's neighbours, of ignoring what the BJP says is the security risk posed by Pakistan and China.
India carried out a nuclear test in 1974. Its long-standing policy, called recessed deterrence, has been to say it does not have a nuclear weapon but retains the option to build the bomb.
